#8394. U.S. Trio Make First Snowboard and Ski Descent of a Near-7,000'er in Langtang

American snowboarder Nick Russell and skiers Adam Fabrikant and Billy Haas have just returned from Langtang with a first snowboard and ski descent of the south face of the formidable Dorje Lhakpa (6,966m).

The team climbed the peak, often known as the Langtang Pyramid, in two days in alpine style. They summited on October 20 and rode/skied down via the same line on the south face, while American photographer Blake Gordon and Canadian cinematographer Leo Hoorn filmed from a high camp.

On the summit of Dorje Lhakpa, October 30, 2026. Photo: Nick Russell

“The south face of Dorje was always the goal, and I’d been planning/dreaming of it for over two years,” Nick Russell told ExplorersWeb while on his way to the airport.

The expedition reached base camp on October 6, shortly after an intense storm blanketed Nepal’s mountains with heavy snow. For them, however, the snow was a blessing rather than a curse.

“The cyclone gave our zone some much-needed snow down low, and on the face, it allowed a clean descent (no down climbing, no rappels),” Russell said.

Sickness slowed the beginning of the expedition. “Three out of five of us, myself included, caught COVID,” Russell said. Luckily, the climbers recovered just as the weather cleared and winds dropped, followed by a string of perfect days.

After the descent. Photo: Nick Russell/Instgram

“Adam, Billy, and I all carried our own gear, set the tracks, and climbed in alpine style on the face,” Nick Russell said. The team had hired three Sherpa climbers (Dawa Geljee Sherpa, Kami Sherpa, and Nuri Sherpa) who helped the camera crew get their gear to a high camp, plus a base camp crew, outfitted by Shangri-La Nepal Trek.

High camp at 6,000m on the south face of Dorje Lhakpa. Photo: Nick Russell/Instagram

The line of ascent/descent followed the snow from below 4,500m to Camp 1 (4,900m) by crossing an icefall. According to the team, this was the only real crux of the ascent, due to overhead serac hazard. At least, the exposed section was short — less than an hour.

On the first day of the summit push, the team continued to their high camp at 6,000m, below the col and at the base of the snowy face. Russell recalls the details of the climb as follows:

The south face is quite steep and sustained above the bergshrund, with sustained 45-50˚ and pockets of 55º, we estimate. The face had seen so much sun [over] the past two weeks that the rising conditions were the biggest unknown of the entire project.

We didn’t know whether or not it would be too icy to ride/ski until we got on the face. The snow was mostly firm, pretty much on the brink of being edge-able. It was two tool and crampon climbing the entire way, with no proper rests to take the pack off.

It took about 7.5 hours to climb the face, and we topped out around 1:30 pm. It took roughly 1.5 hours to descend, with breaks for the cameras to reset.

A climber leaves almost no tracks in the hard snow on Dorje Lhakpa. Photo: Nick Russell/Instagram

The three summiters started down from the top at the same time, Russell on snowboard and his partners on skis. It was anything but easy.

“The snow was more firm than I would have liked, but just edgeable enough to hold an edge,” Russell recalls. “Between the altitude, exposure below, steepness, and how firm it was, it was by far the heaviest line I’ve ever ridden.” He added that if the snow had been a little harder, they would have had to rappel down.

The hard snow on the upper sections. Photo: Nick Russell/Instagram

“You always hope for stable, boot-top powder, but that’s rarely the case at high altitude,” Russell explained. “Instead, you make the most of the conditions presented and try to do it as safely as possible.”

He added: “The entire line was a no-fall zone; one lost edge, and it’d be over. Regardless of conditions, it was a dream for all of us to ride off the top of a peak in Nepal.”

After a partial descent, the team spent the night at high camp, hoping to ride some interesting slopes they had spotted earlier, but finally decided to bail the next morning. “We were satisfied,” Russell said. They continued on skis/snowboard all the way down to the moraines below Camp 1 around 4,500m.

Childhood friends Fabrikant and Haas often partner up on major ski expeditions, mainly in Alaska but also in the Himalaya. They climbed and skied both Gasherbrums 1 and 2 without oxygen after climbing them in the same style in 2024, together with Brendan O’Neill.

“They are the strongest partners I’ve ever been in the mountains with,” said Russell, who has also climbed and snowboarded twice in the Indian Himalaya and twice in Nepal.

“I tried Dhaulagiri in 2022 with Blake Gordon and Dan Corn, but the difficult conditions that year coupled with the loss of Hilaree Nelson [who fell to her death while trying to ski down Manaslu] didn’t allow us to make very much progress,” Russell said.

“I’ve always dreamed of riding lines in the Himalaya, and this felt like a major step forward in my personal journey,” he concluded.

While this is the first ski and snowboard descent of Dorje Lhakpa’s south face, the legendary Marco Siffredi snowboarded the west ridge of the mountain in 1999, with Bertrand Delapierre. Siffredi perished shortly afterward on the Hornbein Couloir on Mount Everest. “Dorje Lhakpa first entered my psyche from Marco and Bertrand’s descent,” the rider recalled.

The south face of Dorje Lhakpa was only climbed for the first time in 2021, by Spaniards Mikel Inoriza, Iker Madoz, and Mikel Zabalza.

“I came across a photo of the south face and the American Alpine Journal article from the Spanish team’s first ascent in 2021,” Russell said. “The massive south face is visible from the Kathmandu Valley on a clear day, and it is honestly crazy to me that no one had skied it before.”

“Today,” he went on, “people are so hyper-focused on the 8,000m peaks (for good reason, I get it), but there are still virgin lines waiting for a snowboard/ski descent in the 6,000-7,000m range. It just takes a shit ton of work to make it happen.”

#8391. Saddle to Paddle: Bikerafting From Canada to Mexico

Pete Streufert and his friend Carter (no last name) are cycling 4,025km and packrafting 645km across the U.S. from Canada to Mexico. Starting in Glacier National Park, they will cross four rivers and six U.S. states to finish in El Paso, Texas.

Their route connects the rivers with long-distance cycling trails. This allows the pair to cross landscapes that would usually require separate trips by bike and watercraft. Streufert, a geospatial wildfire scientist and cartographer, came up with the route by combining existing GPS tracks and geographical data from Bikepacking.com, American Whitewater, and OpenStreetMap. He overlaid cycling corridors and rivers to identify where the two could connect.

Before starting the journey on September 17, he said they could find no record of anyone using this particular combination of rivers and cycling routes. So it is possible that they are the first to do so.

They started what they neatly call the Saddle to Paddle Traverse on September 17, from Glacier National Park, Montana, on the Canadian border. They kicked off the first packrafting section with a 115km descent of the North Fork of the Flathead River, which forms part of the western boundary of Glacier National Park.

From there, they followed the Great Divide Mountain Bike Route through Montana toward Jackson Lake, Wyoming, for 1,107km. Here, they hit their second paddling phase on the Snake River.

Every time they reach a river, the pair inflates their rafts, load their bicycles aboard, and paddle downstream. Then at each takeout, they deflate the rafts, attach them to their bikes, and continue riding.

After 130km along the Snake River, their route joined the SLoToJa cycling corridor. They pedaled through Idaho, Wyoming, and Utah. Here, a short connector track took them onto the newly developed Golden Gravel Trail. A further 860km of cycling brought them to Utah’s Green River.

They then paddled 328km through Desolation and Gray Canyons, including a handful of Class III rapids, and their only Class IV rapid of the trip.

Pulling their rafts out in Canyonlands National Park, they took the White Rim Trail to Moab. They are now taking a few days in Moab to “get all the mud off our bikes and escape the rain for a day or two before we keep heading south,” says Streufert.

From here, they will once again pick up the Golden Gravel Trail through the La Sal Mountains and across Colorado, then continue on the Great Divide Mountain Bike Route to New Mexico.

Paddling the Green River. Photo: Pete Streufert

A final paddling section on New Mexico’s Rio Chama will take them to the last leg of the trip, a 950km ride to El Paso.

The pair are riding Rodeo Labs Flaanimal 6.0 Steel, fitted with 29-inch Vittoria Mezcal tires, and using Kokopelli packrafts. The pair have described this as a “self-supported” route, although of course they’re replenishing their food along the way. They seem to combine camping with staying in towns.

View this post on Instagram See this post on Instagram

They should complete the journey within the next few weeks, within their two-month timeline. You can follow their progress here.

#8388. Solo Trekker Flouts Khumbu Rules, Evacuated After Cliff Fall

A 26-year-old Australian solo trekker who fell from a cliff near Lobuche in the Everest region has been evacuated by helicopter to Kathmandu. He is recovering in intensive care. By law, all foreign trekkers are supposed to have a guide in the Khumbu.

Joshua Patrick Cherubino sustained severe head injuries after falling at Kongma La Pass. He was first taken to Lobuche, then flown out on October 27, according to The Tourism Times.

Kongma La, at about 5,535m, is the highest of the trio of high passes on the classic Everest Three Passes circuit. It links the Chhukung side of the Imja Valley with Lobuche over rocky, non-glaciated moraine. The crossing is long and remote; the descent toward Lobuche is often loose underfoot and comes after hours already spent at altitude.

The case has again drawn attention to Nepal’s rules in the Khumbu. Since 2023, the Nepal Tourism Board has required that all foreign trekkers be accompanied by a licensed guide within national parks, including Sagarmatha.

In practice, the local Khumbu Pasang Lhamu Rural Municipality has continued to issue its own permits and has not strictly enforced the national guide requirement. Thus, independent trekking remains common on the main Everest routes. Officials quoted by The Tourism Times described unguided travel in the region as a violation of the mandatory rule and a source of preventable rescues.

Cherubino was traveling alone when he was found. No further details on the circumstances of the fall or his condition have been released beyond the hospital’s assessment that he is recovering.

#8387. SHT Day 13: Wanna Split It?

I was worried how my body would perform today, considering the beating I felt I gave it yesterday. Before I tuck in for the night, I always stretch really well and roll out the sore spots with my little cork ball. Most nights I take some ibuprofen or acetaminophen too, just to help with inflammation.

I’m glad I decided to camp at Middle Gooseberry. The next one was half a mile off trail!

My body felt good when I woke up, and for the most part it held up all day today. Sometimes the knee feels tweaky, and this trip has my left Achilles a little sore, but not bad. A few exercises and stretches have kept that at bay so far. Regarding the knee, I think 90% of it is mental. I have a baseline worry that IT band syndrome will creep back in. If I just distract myself with the surroundings and/or music, walk like a normal human being, then my knee is absolutely fine.

A girl stopped by my campsite this morning before I left. I barely heard her, she was almost totally silent. The little noise I did hear I thought was maybe a squirrel or something. I told her that as she gathered and filtered some water. We laughed about it and I said maybe I’d see her down the trail as I packed up and took off.

The trail this morning first splits a pair of trees.

A few miles later I stopped at a nice shelter called Skunk Creek Shelter, which I think was within Gooseberry Falls State Park. I was having second breakfast and stretching, then sure enough I saw her approach. We chatted for a while, and she told me she was from Alaska. She was in the area for a wedding soon and was trying to make big miles on a time crunch, like 20 per day. She was very nice, but it’s likely I won’t be seeing her again, lol.

A little while later I stopped for L&L (lunch and latrine) at Blueberry Hill Campsite. The guidebook described this site as having unreliable water, but there was a bit of water in a nearly dry creek nearby thanks to the recent rains. I made sure to filter some here, having learned my lesson from yesterday.

This afternoon I passed through Split Rock State Park. The trail takes you way up along the Split Rock River for quite a ways before crossing it to come all the way back down the other side. I didn’t mind this seemingly extra mileage because it was very pretty. The bridge was out where the SHT crosses, but at this time it was easily rock hoppable.

Again, there were four campsites clustered along the river, and the last one would have been such a cool place to stay, but I was only at 10 miles for the day so I kept going. The campsite I’m planning to stay at tonight is dry though, so I made sure to fill up with water again before leaving the river’s easy access.

Walking next to the Split Rock River and all its glory.

Former bridge site. I was able to rock hop across the water just a few feet downstream from here.

I stopped mid-afternoon for a snack at another day use shelter. This one was pretty dilapidated, but it had a great view. In fact, I’ve had great views for most of the day. In addition, the weather today has been warm and nice, and the trail has been forgiving.

A little after 5 pm I rolled into camp at Chapins Ridge Campsite. As the name suggests, it rests up on a pretty little ridge away from any creeks or rivers, but it was surrounded by big, beautiful pines and soft pine needles completely covered the ground. This will do nicely. There was nobody else here, but this site was giving off good vibes.

Tonight’s dinner was a homemade Pad Thai with a Thai flavored tuna packet. It was ok. I definitely prefer just a plain chicken packet in that meal. I was able to connect with my husband for a bit and confirm our meetup spot for tomorrow. He’s all packed and ready to drive up, and I’m excited to see him!

#8384. West Ridge or Hornbein Couloir? Everest Team Prepares for Fourth Attempt

The Russian team is preparing to head up Everest’s West Ridge for a fourth time. While no easy option exists, they want to avoid the extremely exposed, difficult, and uncertain ridge route. Their only alternative is the Hornbein Couloir, which would force them to stray temporarily into Tibet.

Andrei Vasiliev, Vitaly Shipilov, and Sergey Kondrashkin are in Kathmandu recovering from a viral infection and waiting out Cyclone Arnab, which is now weakening. They will return to their base in Lobuche this weekend, determined to climb Everest without supplemental oxygen.

Everest West Ridge some days ago. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev

“So far, we have completed three rotations on the mountain,” leader Vasiliev told ExplorersWeb. “Part of this time was spent exploring different options for accessing the route.”

The Russian team has a permit to climb Everest from Nepal, as long as they attempt a route other than the standard Khumbu Icefall-South Col-Southeast Ridge. This has become the normal South Side route since Hillary and Tenzing’s first ascent in 1953.

Topo of the Russian team’s planned route on Everest, courtesy of Andrei Vasiliev

First, the Russians tried to bypass the Khumbu Icefall via the Nuptse Shoulder toward Camp 1, but heavy snow forced them to find another route. Crossing the Icefall (sharing paths with the normal route) was also too hard in the deep snow and on the shaky snow bridges over the innumerable crevasses.

“Eventually, we selected a third option, via the Lho La,” Vasiliev said. “From that pass, our planned route continues across the West Shoulder, along the West Ridge.”

At the Lho La col. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev

On their latest foray, the team reached 6,400m. “We climbed approximately twelve 60m pitches over rock, snow, and ice of moderate difficulty,” said Vasiliev.

He noted that on the way to the West Shoulder, they found traces of previous expeditions, including old ropes and snow anchors.

As for the terrain ahead of them, Vasiliev said:

From our highest point reached, the terrain ahead looks manageable. We can see two more steep rock steps, each approximately 100m high, along with possible bypasses on steep snow slopes. Beyond these obstacles, the terrain appears easier, and we hope to be able to move simultaneously.

Rocky section on the way to Everest’s West Ridge. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev

Vasiliev and his team are confident they can manage this route, despite doing so in increasingly wintry conditions.

The route linking the Lho La, the West Shoulder, and the West Ridge of Everest has been completed only twice. A Yugoslavian team led by Tone Skarja did the first complete ascent in 1979. They used the Hornbein Couloir variation on their descent.

The only repetition was done by a Bulgarian team in 1984. Hristo Prodanov reached the summit on his own and retraced his steps down the ridge but never made it back alive. Some of his partners who summited days later descended via the normal route. Three other teams who climbed the West Shoulder-West Ridge summited by traversing to the North Face, on the Chinese side, and climbing the Hornbein Couloir.

The North Face of Everest from the West Shoulder. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev

Objectively speaking, the Hornbein Couloir offers more summit (and survival) chances than the upper part of the West Ridge. However, it requires traversing into Chinese territory. The Russian team has a permit to climb only from Nepal. It is unclear if a brief border trespass could be considered, and Vasiliev has not confirmed what they will do. “First we need to complete one more rotation,” he said.

#8381. Photo Contest Winners Reveal Amazing Microscopic Worlds

Since 1975, Nikon’s Small World competition has featured images produced by optical microscopes, an art that usually stays in scientific papers and textbooks. But through the carefully engineered lenses of the microscope, photomicrographers sometimes capture glimpses of strikingly surreal, alien beauty. The 2026 Photomicrography Competition winners include subjects both living and mechanical, small and very small.

The fruiting bodies of a Hemitrichia slime mold remind one distinctly of Dr. Seuss. Photo: Eric Epstein/Nikon Small World

The winning image shows bubbling globules of black ink being injected onto a piece of paper by an inkjet printer. Behind the lens was 25-year-old German design student Ole Bielfeldt, whose work explores the surprising complexity of everyday objects. His process is largely DIY: Bielfeldt builds his own setups, cobbles together parts, and learns techniques online.

“I just pick somewhere to start and go for it,” Bielfeldt explained. “You’re likely going to fail at first, and that’s what makes it even more interesting.”

The experimentation and imperfection, he added, are the most interesting parts of the process and, ultimately, more important to him than achieving the highest image quality.

Ah, mice; the humble martyrs to scientific progress. A significant amount of science seems to involve cutting up mice and learning from the result. But in this sort of photography, even the strongest mouse advocate must admit that the results are visually spectacular.

Satu Paavonsalo and Dr. Sinem Karaman of the University of Helsinki took this image of a mouse’s eye while researching drug therapy. Photo: Satu Paavonsalo and Dr. Sinem Karaman/Nikon Small World

Third place went to another rodent part: a 5X-magnified image of neurons in a mouse’s brain.

Photo: Kaelin Wulf and Rachel Flannery/Nikon Small World

In defense of humanity, we were also willing to subject our own body parts to photographic investigation. The 7th-place winner came from Dr. Bruno Cisterna and Dr. Eric Vitriol at the Medical College of Georgia at Augusta University. Using confocal imaging, which involves scanning a specimen to generate optical sections, they captured human neurons at 20X magnification.

These human neurons were grown from reprogrammed skin cells. Photo: Dr. Bruno Cisterna and Dr. Eric Vitriol/Nikon Small World

I’ll end with a personal favorite of mine, John-Oliver Dum’s image of a little jumping spider, dusted with pollen. Dum, who won second place, credits a childhood bite for his fascination with spiders. The pollen was cultivated by his wife, specifically to create images like this one.

You can disagree, but I think this little guy is adorable. Photo: John-Oliver Dum

You can view the full gallery of winners and honorable mentions here. If you want to see photos of larger things, check out the winners from the Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026, Aerial Photography, 2026 Ocean Photographer of the Year, or Memorial Maria Luisa International Photo and Video competitions.

#8380. Mother and Daughter Killed in Suspected Grizzly Bear Attack in British Columbia

Authorities in British Columbia are investigating a suspected fatal grizzly bear attack after a mother, 48, and her 20-year-old daughter were found dead near Bella Coola this week.

Jennifer Balcarras and her daughter, Selah Reed, were initially reported missing on November 1 after failing to return from what was supposed to be a brief afternoon walk. A joint search effort involving the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, local search and rescue teams, and the British Columbia Conservation Officer Service led to the discovery of Balcarras’s body on Monday afternoon in the Snooka West Trail area. Reed’s remains were located the following day.

B.C. Conservation Officer Service Inspector Jeff Tyre stated that wildlife officials are actively working to locate and capture any animals connected to the incident, adding that it is unclear whether more than one bear was involved. If a captured bear is linked to the fatal encounter, it will be euthanized in accordance with the province’s public safety protocols for human-wildlife conflicts.

Officials have urged the public to avoid the Snooka West Trail area during the ongoing investigation.

Relatives described the mother and daughter as exceptionally close. Josh Balcarras, Balcarras’s brother, has said that the two shared many interests, telling reporters that Selah frequently enjoyed hiking with her mother. Jennifer Balcarras had recently relocated to Bella Coola for a career change and to start a new chapter in her life. She is survived by three young adult children and a grandchild.

Family members described Reed as just beginning her journey into adulthood, “with her whole life ahead of her.”

Because Balcarras’s recent move had drained her savings, her family has launched a GoFundMe campaign to assist with funeral expenses.

The B.C. Ministry of Environment, Lands and Parks estimates the grizzly bear population in the province to be between 10,000 and 13,000. While the ministry notes that human-grizzly conflicts are uncommon and typically occur when a bear is startled or is defending food or cubs, the region has seen a troubling string of violent encounters over the last few years.

In November 2025, an aggressive grizzly attacked a group of 20 elementary school students and teachers in the Bella Coola Valley, leaving four people with serious or critical injuries. The bear in that incident was never captured.

A month before that, a bear injured two hikers near McGregor Mountain; one victim died weeks later from complications related to their injuries. Other recent incidents include a hunter who was severely injured before fatally shooting a bear in the Elkford region in May 2024, and a 21-year-old woman who survived a defensive attack near Tumbler Ridge in July 2023.

If you encounter a grizzly bear on a trail, remain calm, avoid direct eye contact, speak in a low and steady voice, and slowly back away without turning your back or running. Carry bear spray in an accessible location at all times when hiking in known grizzly territory.

#8377. College Students Found Dead After Hiking Colorado Mountain

The two young men who set off into Colorado’s Sawatch Mountains this month were both passionate about taking the outdoors seriously. One was studying to be a wildland firefighter, while the other hoped to become a mountain guide.

But both of them were found dead Wednesday, under circumstances that remain unclear. Local authorities spent days looking for missing hikers Kaden Matsuda, 19, and Jackson Donlon, 20.

The bodies were finally discovered near West Apostle Mountain on October 28, just outside of Gunnison, Colorado.

Matsuda and Donlon, students at Colorado Mountain College in Leadville, had planned on hiking and camping near Ice Mountain, a 13,960-foot peak located about 50 miles from Gunnison.

They left for their trip on Oct. 23. College staff notified local authorities they were missing on Oct. 26, according to the Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office. The men’s families said they were both experienced hikers.

Matsuda was studying to be a wildland firefighter, and Donlon was training to become a mountain guide.

Kaden Matsuda, left, and Jackson Donlon. Supplied: Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office

Kaden Matsuda, left, and Jackson Donlon. Supplied: Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office

Search-and-rescue teams were deployed and found their vehicle at the trailhead. Weather conditions looked risky, with heavy snow falling in Chaffee County.

“Ice Mountain is a very technical climb, and it is recommended that hikers be very experienced when trying to tackle it. That is when it is dry. Although there was only about eight inches of snow around Kaden’s vehicle and in the lower basin, Ice Mountain received one to two feet of snow,” the sheriff’s office said in a Facebook post.

Multiple local SAR teams worked on the case. Photo: Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office

Multiple local SAR teams worked on the case. Photo: Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office

Rescue teams used drones, helicopters, and dogs to search for the two hikers. On October 27, they located their tent, which had collapsed under the weight of the snow, near West Apostle Mountain (13,597 feet). Inside were sleeping bags, stoves, and other equipment, but the two men were nowhere to be found.

The next day, authorities announced they had found their bodies in the mountain’s basin. Officials declined to share potential causes of death, beyond stating that they did not suspect foul play.

The Sawatch Range of the Rocky Mountains is home to many 13,000- and 14,000-foot peaks. Some of them, like West Apostle Mountain, require technical climbing ability and become substantially more difficult and dangerous during wet weather. The route up the mountain requires traversing fields of loose boulder scree and talus that can be hazardous after snow.

From 2010 to 2017, eight people have died in the Sawatch Mountains. Falls are the most common cause of fatalities for those tackling Colorado’s 13ers and 14ers, as the state’s highest mountains are known to locals.

#8374. How to Skin a Deer Like a Pro

Published Oct 26, 2026 9:38 AM EDT

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

If you ask a dozen hunters how to skin a deer, you’ll find that every one of them does something slightly different. While that may be frustrating for newer hunters, it should also be reassuring: There’s no one right way or right order to skin a deer. As long as you follow the general techniques and handy tips outlined below, you’ll be able to skin a deer in no time.

Once you do get the hang of it, skinning a deer is quick and easy. Butchering and packaging a deer can take all afternoon but “if it takes me 10 minutes to skin a deer,” says Cheyne Matzenbacher, a one-time deer processor and current deer outreach specialist for the National Deer Association, “that’s a long time.”

Read through the whole article or click on a topic below to jump ahead.

Although there are lots of tools and setups that can make skinning a deer much easier, the only thing you really need is a sharp knife. The best skinning knives are typically handy enough for maneuvering but durable enough for joint work. There’s nothing wrong with using a small folding skinning knife in the backcountry or a longer filet knife. Just don’t use a dull knife — it’s dangerous and takes longer to finish the job.

Before you can skin your deer, you need to gut or field dress your deer, which involves removing the internal organs from the chest and abdominal cavities. Once your deer is gutted, you’ll ideally want to hang it. It’s certainly possible to skin your deer on the ground or the bed of your pickup (I’ve done both many times), and if you plan to do this, you should study up on the gutless method of skinning deer and other big game. This process is preferred by backcountry hunters who quarter their deer in the field, slip the meat into game bags, and pack it back to camp or their trucks.

But for most whitetail hunters and Western hunters who hunt close to home, it’s easier and faster to skin a deer that’s hanging. The meat will also stay cleaner if it’s hanging instead of touching dirt, bacteria, and deer hair on, say, your tailgate. There are a dozen methods for hanging a deer, and they all depend on your location and the tools available to you.

Deer hunters are divided on this question. You can skin a deer that’s hanging head up or head down, but there are advantages to each method. When Matzenbacher worked as a deer processor for a season, he and his coworkers would hang deer by the head or neck to skin the animal, then flip it to hang head-down for butchering.

“Think about how a deer jumps over a fence: His legs are folded up against his body. Let gravity help you, and let the natural way a deer is going to fold up help you skin it,” says Matzenbacher. “Don’t fight it.”

I skin all my deer head-down, so that’s how I’ll walk you through this example. If you want to try the head-up method, the principles are all the same. Just start at the neck and work your way down. If you are planning to shoulder mount your deer, don’t follow all of these instructions; you’ll need to make very careful cuts near the forelegs and chest. These traditional instructions are for does or for bucks you plan to skull cap or Euro mount. Finally, redneck ingenuity abounds when it comes to skinning deer, and if you’re interested in working smarter, not harder, consider the golf-ball trick or skinning your deer with your truck.

Make identical circular cuts near the knee joints, circling the thin bone of the lower leg on the side closer to the hoof. (This is the only time you should be cutting down on deer hair. For all the rest of the cuts, insert your knife under the hide and cut parallel to the meat or away from the meat.)

Slip the tip of your knife under the hide inside one hind leg. Applying even pressure, cut up and out in a single smooth motion as you run your blade toward the pelvis until you reach the cut you made while field dressing. Do this on the other hind leg, then start to skin the hide away from the tendons where you’re going to put the gambrel and expose the knees. The idea is to remove just enough hide that you don’t have to skin around the metal of the gambrel once you hang the deer.

Thread the gambrel through the natural holes you just exposed in the hind legs (between the bone and thick tendon) and hoist your deer. Tie it off at a comfortable height to work on the hindquarters

Note: You can perform this at almost any point in the process. Some hunters prefer to do this before hanging their deer, others do it as needed throughout the process (as pictured). You can also use loppers or a reciprocating saw for this and may want a saw for the hind legs; just take care not to cut the big tendon on the hind legs.

Slightly bend the front legs and cut through the joint. Wiggle the leg to find the weakest point and use your knife blade to cut perpendicularly through the tendons and between the bones until the joint is free. This may seem tricky at first, but it’s simpler than it looks.

Run your knife between the lower leg cuts and the cut along the abdomen you made while field dressing. Do this on both sides of the inner hindquarters. Combined with the lower leg cuts (or removal) these are the major cuts that will allow you to skin most of your deer.

Using your off hand to lift the hide and your knife hand to make cuts parallel to the meat, begin to peel away the hide. Work from the inside of the hind leg around to the outside. Do this on both sides.

Separate the hide at the tail by either running your knife under the hide and pulling it off the tail like yanking off a sock, or cutting the tail off altogether. Use your knife to work between the joints or simply saw it off.

Now you can begin the easiest part of skinning a deer: letting gravity help you pull the hide off. You may need to raise the deer a little for this part. Once you’ve used your knife to separate the hide from the tail and the inside of the hind legs, set it aside and grab fist-fulls of hide. Using your body weight, pull the hide toward the ground. If the hide doesn’t pull free in places, you can use your knife to help release the hide by slicing the delicate white crackly tissue that connects the skin to the meat. You’ll likely need to do this around the belly area and occasionally along the back

The hide will start to form a tube as you peel it away and it gets closer to the chest and neck.

Before the hide gets in your way too much and starts to drape over the forelegs, make cuts inside the forelegs similar to the ones you made on the hindlegs, starting near the knee joint and running the blade along the backs of the legs until they reach the body and chest. (If you didn’t remove the lower forelegs before, be sure to do this before you try to pull the hide over it.) You can also just pull the skin over the forelegs by pushing down on the hide between the brisket and front of the cut front legs (see video above). It’s similar to pulling off a sock.

Continue to work the hide down over the shoulders and forelegs like you’re peeling off a sweatshirt. The cuts you made on the legs will appear and you can use your knife to free the hide.

Once the hide is over the shoulders, use your knife to separate it from the neck. The freed hide will be heavy now and starting to get in your way. Use its weight to your advantage so it pulls the at the hide still connected to the deer.

When you reach the base of the neck, use a saw or your knife to sever the head from the vertebrae. You’ll have to cut through meat and tendons on all sides until you reach the spine. If you’re using a knife, work through the vertebrae like you did with the knee joints, turning the deer’s head a little bit to help free space between the vertebrae. You want to make your cut at the atlas joint, the connection between the head and the first vertebra of the neck and spinal column.

Once you cut through the neckbone the hide should be completely removed from your deer, though still attached to the head. If you need to get your deer tested for CWD or plan to make a European mount, just slice away all that extra hide hanging off the head.

This step is only necessary if you plan to make your own skull mount. Start at the neck and cut away the skin as you did on the rest of the deer, making cuts parallel to the meat and skull until you’ve removed most of the skin. A flathead screwdriver can help free the hide at the base of a buck’s pedicles, which can be the trickiest part to remove. This is a more time consuming process and should be done carefully to avoid injury or scoring the skull with your knife, which can cause cosmetic damage.

No, you don’t have to hang a deer to skin it. I’ve skinned plenty of deer in the back of a pickup, and sometimes that’s your only option if you’re hunting in areas without many trees or access to a barn or meat pole. It’s definitely easier to skin a deer if it’s hanging since gravity helps remove the hide. It’s also easier to keep the meat clean if your deer is hanging when you skin it; skinning a deer on a level surface like a tailgate or outdoor table makes it more likely that you’ll get deer hair and possibly dirt or bacteria on the meat.

The only tool you must have to skin a deer is a reasonably sharp knife. There are plenty of additional tools that make the job easier, and those will depend on where you’re skinning your deer. If you’re working in the field, consider a hitch hoist for your vehicle and a pair of loppers to quickly remove legs. If you have the luxury of a garage, shed, or barn to hang your deer, along with electricity, you might invest in an electric winch and a Sawzall.

How fast you need to skin a deer depends on a few factors, including the temperature outside and your state’s carcass transportation laws. As a general rule, in the right conditions (cool and dry), a deer can hang hide-on for several weeks. (See below for more details.) If it’s hot and humid, skin the deer as fast as you can to help cool the meat and prevent spoilage. If temperatures are near or below freezing, you should skin a deer while the carcass is still warm and the hide is pliable; skinning a frozen deer is both difficult and time consuming. Meanwhile, CWD laws in your state may require you to debone all deer meat before crossing county or state lines. If such regulations apply where you hunt or live, you’re going to need to skin your deer so you can debone it before you hit the road.

A skinned deer can hang for up to a few weeks if it’s stored in the proper conditions. The deer needs to stay cool and dry, such as sheltered outside during the winter or (preferably) inside a walk-in cooler set to a consistent temperature. Experts recommend hanging deer for 7 to 10 days at a temperature between 35 and 45 degrees to allow enzymes to age, or tenderize, the meat. A deer will not age properly if it’s frozen.

Yes, you can age deer meat with the skin on. Opinions on this vary about which method (aging venison with or without the hide) is better. Any meat that’s exposed to air as it ages will develop a dried crust, and the hide can help protect that meat from drying. I once hung a doe, hide-on, in a walk in-cooler with the temperature set to 38 degrees for two weeks. It was surprisingly easy to skin after aging and I lost less meat than when I age completely skinned quarters. But if you let your deer hang for much longer than that (three weeks or more) the meat may over-tenderize and start to come away with the hide, forcing you to work slowly and possibly wasting meat. Still, letting deer meat hang for at least a day or more can help keep it dry, tenderize the venison, and concentrate flavor before butchering.

The best deer skinning knife is a sharp one. The type of knife—skinning, caping, boning, or filet—matters less than its sharpness and the cuts you make. Many hunters and wild game processors prefer different types of knives for different stages of the skinning process: There are skinning knives (usually slim, handy knives with a sturdy blade), flexible filet knives for working around awkward angles or different muscle groups, caping knives for skinning the shoulders and head of a trophy deer, and stout boning knives for separating knee joints. Try several types of knives to find the best deer skinning knife for you.

Remember, there is no single perfect way to skin a deer. Every deer hunter and processor I’ve met does something slightly different, and most swear their way is the best way. Find which tools and techniques work for how you hunt and what kind of facilities you have access to (if any). The only way to truly learn how to skin a deer is, well, to skin a deer. So sharpen your knife and get after it.

Natalie Krebs is the Executive Editor of Outdoor Life, where she tackles everything from reporting digital features to producing podcast episodes. Originally from Missouri, she currently lives in northwest Arkansas with her bird dog, Hatchet.

#8373. Am I Done Here? — John Muir Trail Day 6

The night before our last hike to Sam’s car at Onion Valley I awoke and recorded the following.  It is only lightly edited:

Some thoughts in the middle of the night. It’s one a.m.  In a few hours we’ll be going over Kearsarge Pass. That’s not a walk in the park.

It’s over 2,000 feet of elevation gain. Maybe around 10 miles of hiking and then going off trail. I have to think this is probably it for me.

I am exhausted. I have been coughing and blowing my nose for six days, and for six weeks before these six days. I’m just running out of juice.

I cannot imagine coming back on trail until I’ve gone at least 24 hours without coughing once, without blowing my nose once.  And I don’t know when that will happen because it feels like it’ll never happen.  I mean, six weeks?  This thing’s been going on and on and on.

Thank God I’ve had the energy to get up and over these passes at all, but I have.  And I appreciate Sam so much.  He’s been such a great companion, so positive, so upbeat, so helpful in every way.

I really don’t think I could have made it without him. I don’t know what I would  have done, but I’ve had enough.  I just don’t see how I can come back out here without serious health improvement.

So, I have to figure out what to do.  I don’t think I’ll even talk to Sam about this until after we go over the top of Kearsarge Pass.  When we’re going downhill, I will be confident that I’ll actually make it out of here.

But no, I’m not really worried about not getting out of here, I just need time to ponder what to do.  I’d go with Sam to the airport in Las Vegas and fly home, but I don’t have a passport.  It’s with son Gabriel in Santa Rosa, California.

And my driver’s license is not a RealID driver’s license.  So, I’m hosed, I can’t fly, but that’s fine.  I could take a bus, whatever, I can figure that out.

I just gotta get better and then reappraise.  You know, if I were 30 years old, I’d say, screw it, I’ll just come back next year and try again, no biggie. But I’m not 30, I’m 69.

I’m in remission from cancer.  No one says I’m cured, but of course I hope it’s a long-term remission, naturally.

I’ve got a son with recurrent colon cancer, that came back less than two months after he finished his chemotherapy treatment.  That’s shocking and scary.

I’ve got a wife who went in for a routine appendectomy, they took out a healthy appendix, and now she is suffering.  I don’t really know what is going on there, because she can’t or won’t tell me the details.

And I’ve got to wrap up a whole bunch of different things, finish my taxes, finish my dead mother’s taxes, deal with some other stuff in my life.

The bottom line is six days of coughing and coughing, six days of blowing my nose, six days of giant, ugly, sticky mucus wads coming out of my nose and out of my chest when I cough; it’s just… it’s exhausting.  I can’t believe I made it up Mount Whitney and over Forester Pass.  It’s just astounding that I did those things given the condition I was in.

But I’ve had enough. I can’t just turn around and go back on trail.  Not the way I’m feeling.

After making that recording, I was able to get a little sleep despite peeing several more times in the night and still coughing.

The morning was cold and I said to Sam, “Let’s hold off on leaving until later,  when it’s a little bit warmer.”  That plan turned out to be necessary because our gear was pretty wet from the rain.

Sam at our camp site; you can tell it was cold by his outfit.

So we took a fairly leisurely time breaking camp, digging our cat holes, and eating breakfast, but also drying out my groundsheet which lay on a pretty wet spot overnight.

I realized in the middle of the night, checking my FarOut app, that the first mile and a half of hiking was going to entail about a thousand feet of elevation gain.  It is always better to be prepared than to be surprised by these things.  As we headed out, we were ready to sweat right away.

It was hard, but not impossibly hard, not terribly hard.  We got up those thousand feet and then the trail toward Bullfrog Lake was a series of gentle ups and downs.   It was so beautiful.  I mean, the views were stunningly, jaw-droppingly, beautiful.

At one point we saw a couple of bucks browsing by the trail.  Our presence didn’t seem to bother them too much. They didn’t run away; they kept browsing.

Bucks browsing — they kind of blend in, don’t they?

We also saw a hand-written sign warning of bears in the vicinity.

I especially like the part about “chase it like you are trying to catch and eat it!”

We continued on.  When we got to Bullfrog Lake, we actually went for a swim.

Bullfrog Lake (I think, there were a series of lakes up there…)

It was funny, because when Sam proposed the swim, I said, “Don’t you think I would have to be crazy to go for a swim in a cold mountain lake with a bad cough?”

He replied, “Oh, you mean not something sensible like climbing Mount Whitney with a cough, right?”

I had to admit; he had a point.  I stripped down and went in.

The swim actually felt really good, really fresh.  I just put on my water shoes, swam 10 yards out, swam 10 yards back, and got out.  It was a nice sunny day, so drying out was very fast, very easy.

While at Bullfrog Lake we filtered water and loaded up for the hot hike up to the pass.

We ate our lunch in that spot and then continued hiking up and up and up.

At no point was the elevation gain so difficult that I felt overwhelmed.  I just used my usual technique.  I’d count 60 paces while climbing, or I’d count 30 if it was very steep, and then I’d stop to take a series of deep breaths to slow my heartbeat and catch my breath.  But I was still coughing, still honking up a bunch of nasty mucus.

The views ascending made the climb easier…

Eventually we made it to Kearsarge Pass.  Along with a bunch of other folks going in both directions, we celebrated our accomplishment.  The views from there were glorious.  Looking across at the teeth of the mountains, the raw majesty of it was wonderful.  Those “teeth” are depicted in the feature image at the top of this post.  Even the pass itself was special.

The rocks in the pass don’t look very stable, do they?

It was four miles straight down, which meant four miles straight up if I were to return to trail.  I wondered whether I would.  We passed some beautiful lakes, such as Gilbert Lake, on the way down.  The trail also passed through a vast tumble of giant boulders.

Gilbert Lake is popular because they say it is full of fish.

As we emerged from the boulders, we finally could see the road down below, and the car park where Sam’s rental was parked.  It seemed really close when I first saw the car park.  I thought, “Oh, we’re going to be there in 15 minutes.”

See the road down there? With Independence, CA behind it.

The visual distance was deceptive; it was more like an hour before we got there.  But eventually we got to the car park.  The car was fine, everything there was fine.  Arriving was a huge relief.

As we started driving down the hillside, I told Sam, “Look, I really feel like I need to have 24 hours of no cough and no nasty mucus before I go back on this trail, because I just can’t do it.”  Fighting my health and trying to struggle up mountain passes at the same time was just too hard for me.

Repeatedly over two days on the trail we tried to book a cabin at Lauralyn’s Williamson Motel by texting her husband Doug from my Garmin.  We could not get through and were very frustrated by it.  When we drove up to the motel in Independence, I learned we had the wrong number.  It started with 760, not the 750 I was given.  To be clear, I got it second-hand, not from Lauralyn herself, so I am not suggesting we were deliberately misled.  In any case, there was “no room at the inn.”

Doug was nice enough and answered my questions.  In particular, I wanted to know where to go for medical treatment.  The South Inyo Hospital was in Lone Pine and North Inyo Hospital was in Bishop.  Doug suggested that Bishop would have a little more to offer, especially if I needed a pharmacy.  So even though it was a longer drive, we decided to go north.

The other advantage to going north was a barbeque joint Doug recommended.  It was the Copper Top BBQ in Big Pine, halfway to Bishop.  I was already salivating.

Sam spoke with his wife Mary while I was sorting this out and then I called Lee as we drove north.  I found out she had the same respiratory infection that was afflicting me.   It seemed to be affecting her even worse, mostly because of her appendectomy.  Every time she coughed it pulled at the healing adhesions within her abdomen.  So, it was really causing her a lot of pain and difficulty, and she was on a lot of medications.  Despite this, she said she was all right if I chose to stay on the trail.  She even encouraged me.

As I spoke to her, I actually shed some tears when I expressed my gratitude to Sam for his help and support.

Then we got to the Copper Top BBQ.  Oh my God.  There was a menu item that included two of everything, everything doubled.  I mean, tri-tip, pulled pork, chicken sausage, ribs, and everything!  I imagine a lot of people take some home.  Sam and I finished the whole damn thing.  It was so good.  The barbecue was great; the coleslaw was excellent; they had a chili bean dish that was fantastic.

We had the Big Pine Mega Platter (2 Person) — soooo good!

Then we made our way to Bishop.  Doug suggested either the Best Western or the Motel 6.   They were next door to each other, so we pulled into the Best Western. The woman behind the desk was on the phone; she wouldn’t even make eye contact.  We waited and waited and waited.  She was still talking, still not looking at us.  Then we heard her say, “Yeah, okay, you have a room for today for $250.”

We were like, what the hell?  No, not in Bishop, California.  So, we left Ms. No-Eye-Contact to go next door to the Motel 6.  The price was about a hundred bucks less.  We got our rooms for the night.

Even after the barbeque, we went next door for milkshakes before calling it a night.  I planned to go to North Inyo Hospital the next morning.

I actually took a bath.  In undressing I discovered my shorts had an embarrassing  tear in them in the front.  Apparently, nobody noticed, or else they were too polite to say anything.  Then I got in the tub and soaked in water that started clean but rapidly began to look like a mudbath.  I even had to shower off when I got out.

The first night off the trail in Bishop, CA I awoke and recorded the following in my hotel room.  It is only lightly edited:

Here it is now the middle of the night.  It’s actually 3:45 in the morning.  I am still coughing.  I still have mucus.

Maybe it is a little less?  Still, it does not start a 24-hour clock without symptoms.

I will go to the hospital tomorrow.  I guess it has to be the Emergency Room.  Have them look at me and assess the situation.  I am guessing the answer might be, “Well, you’ve got a bad viral infection, and you just have to wait it out.”

If that’s the case, maybe one more chance would be to try to see if there is much more improvement by tomorrow night?  If it’s clear then, maybe I can get back on the trail day after tomorrow?  Sam could drop me off before heading to Las Vegas, or I could spend another zero day, probably in Independence?

It’s not clear cut.  It really is not clear cut.  I don’t know.

I’m very confused.  I feel somewhat drained.  You know, when you embark on one of these journeys, you want to have energy and enthusiasm.  And as long as I’m still coughing and honking, I’m not sure I can conjure that up.  We will see.

Plus, I haven’t even opened my resupply box retrieved from Sam’s car.  I thought of it as too daunting.

I haven’t even thrown out my trash from the first leg of our journey.  So there are a lot of details to pick up here as well.  And I don’t even know what time the checkout is in the morning.

A lot of things to worry about.  At least I am charging my electronics.  That is great.  Now, let me go back to sleep.

#8372. Rock Spire Collapses at Popular Turkish Tourist Site, Killing Three

Part of a rock spire known as a fairy chimney collapsed yesterday near the entrance to one of Turkey’s most popular tourist destinations, killing three people and injuring five others.

The incident occurred around 3:15 pm local time in the town of Goreme, in central Turkey’s Cappadocia region yesterday. Rocks broke away and fell onto people near the parking area. The site is part of a UNESCO World Heritage landscape, famous for its cave dwellings and cone-shaped rock formations. Nevsehir Governor Huseyin Kok said that heavy rainfall triggered a landslide that caused the rocks to detach from the formation, according to Reuters.

Rescue teams initially recovered two bodies from the rubble before discovering a third victim overnight, bringing the death toll to three. The deceased include two Turkish citizens and one foreign national. Five others were injured in the collapse. Some of them were later discharged from hospital, according to AFP.

Eyewitnesses described a loud noise followed by a large dust cloud. The area was closed to the public, and search operations concluded overnight under floodlights.

Turkish Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said an investigation by the chief prosecutor’s office, along with expert assessments, would begin. The collapse occurred on Turkey’s Republic Day, a public holiday when visitor numbers were high.

Cappadocia, in central Anatolia, is renowned for its distinctive fairy chimneys. These tall, thin spires of soft volcanic rock topped by harder caps were shaped over millions of years by wind and water erosion. The Goreme Open-Air Museum and surrounding sites were put on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1985 for their blend of natural landforms and human history, including Byzantine rock-cut churches and underground settlements. The region’s soft rock is geologically fragile and prone to weathering and occasional rockfalls, particularly after heavy rain.

Turkish authorities have previously carried out restoration and monitoring work to address erosion and climate-related risks, and smaller non-fatal collapses were recorded in the area in 2024 and 2025. The site remains one of Turkey’s most visited destinations, drawing tourists for hot-air balloon rides, hiking, and exploration of its unique geology and heritage.

#8369. An Old-School Snowshoe Hare Hunt With Hounds Is the Most Underrated Winter Adventure

Published Oct 26, 2026 11:21 AM EDT

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

One of the things I like about snowshoe hare hunting is hot raspberry pie. Few restaurants serve it, especially in the dead of winter in a northern Michigan small-town cafe. One morning last February, my three hunting partners watched with interest, chins resting on their palms, as I sank a fork into the delicacy.

“Do you always eat raspberry pie for breakfast?” wondered Ralph Holsinger, who had invited me to join their hunting group.

“Only when I find a restaurant sensible enough to serve it.”

Another thing I like about hunting snowshoe or varying hares is trying to figure where they will appear ahead of the bawling pack of hounds. It’s a game of constant adjustment—moving up, moving over, squatting low to see through thick cover. You have to take into account the lay of the land and its habitat types and be able to sort out the hound music from what’s hot and what’s not. Sometimes the elastic circles the hares and hounds run are wide, and sometimes they are deceptively narrow.

Playing your hunches is also important because, after all, hares rarely do what they are supposed to do. That’s what Holsinger says, anyway, and he should know: He has been chasing the all-white bunnies for 50 years.

After leaving the restaurant, the four of us took stands along a fire lane through young jack-pine woods that flanked a cedar swamp. In quick succession, two separate hares gave me the slip. The first time I heard the dogs mushing through the snow toward me, I sneaked 20 yards to my left for a better shooting position. But I should have moved 40 yards because when the bounding bigfoot suddenly appeared, it was too far away for a shot. Joe Covert, a member of our hunting party, ended that romp when he shot the hare as it tried to cross the opening. Then, during the second chase, I should have stayed put; this time the elusive hare practically ran over my earlier position, but I wasn’t quick enough for a shot. It slipped by the other hunters, too, and now the pack had driven the snowshoe deep into the swamp.

We waited, 100 yards apart, and shuffled our feet against the cold. Thirty minutes passed, and now it was 10:30. Then I could hear it—the faint squeal of Squeaky, Holsinger’s lead beagle. Soon, Rambo barked in with a coarse bawl. The stretched-to-the-limit circle was tightening once again. The other dogs—Shane, Twinkie, Candy and John—began to cut loose with assorted chops, yelps and squeals that were definitely growing louder. The gutsy pack of hounds was pushing this splayfoot right down my throat. For once, I wouldn’t have to move at all.

Sinking to haunches, I swept the woods slowly from left to right and waited for the hare to materialize. You never hear snowshoe hares, at least not with snow on the ground, and certainly not with the hounds chorus ringing through the woods and in your ears. No, like true ghosts, snowshoes take shape before your eyes. Suddenly, and with a rush of adrenalin, they are there. So where was this one? The dogs were closing in too fast. Already I could see their skinny tails whipping left and right, but no rabbit.

There comes a point when the hunter of hares knows he has failed, and usually that is when he sees the dogs. They filed by at 30 yards, eagerly punching their noses in and out of the loose snow and ignoring me altogether. How did they know I was no threat to any swamp ghosts today? Snow-choked cedars muffled a shotgun blast, which told me that one of the other hunters, probably Marty Anthony, had ended this nonsense. So much for my hunches.

Seven species of hares—which actually differ from rabbits because they are born fully furred and with eyes open—are native to North America. The snowshoe, or so-called varying hare, turns all white in the winter and is the smallest. At an average of 14 to 15 inches, hares are a little longer than cottontail rabbits. At an average weight of 3 1/2 to four pounds, they are a bit heavier, too. Range of the hare includes the northern tier of states and all of Canada and Alaska. They also live in mountainous regions of the Alleghenies, California and New Mexico. Besides Alaska, 20 states have hunting seasons.

In addition to mysterious population swings that affect both rabbits and hares every 10 years or so, snowshoe numbers rise and fall dramatically according to habitat availability. In areas of aggressive timber-cutting activities or where fire has destroyed a forest, hares thrive on the new growth for a few years. Then, when the forest begins to mature, the animals may all but disappear.

According to Ben Tullar, a wildlife biologist with the New York Department of Environmental Conservation, abandoned farms in northern New York first support red spruce, balsam fir and white cedar. These conifer species get a head start on hardwoods such as maples, beech, yellow birch, black cherry and white ash. “For example, after a period of only five to 15 years,” Tullar said, “an abandoned pasture can support a huntable hare population for another five to 15 years. But the hardwoods eventually overtake the conifers, and a hardwood/softwood mixed forest develops with little understory vegetation and, consequently, no food or shelter for hares.”

When the habitat is right, populations explode because few animals are as prolific as snowshoe hares.

Snowshoe hares are an important food source for hawks, owls, foxes and coyotes. Apparently, hunting by man has little impact on their populations, and that is why seasons in most states are long and bag limits are usually liberal. Wisconsin hunters, for example, have enjoyed no closed seasons and no bag limits since 1965. During peak years, though, they shoot only about 3 percent of the state’s hare population. In Maine, Michigan, Minnesota, Oregon and Washington, hares go underharvested most years.

Hares rarely hole up, a habit that makes them available to hunters on all but the coldest days. In bad weather, they crouch under snow-laden branches and have been known to tunnel under snow, but they don’t usually go underground, even when pushed by a hound pack. Most jumped hares don’t seem to be afraid of the dogs anyway, and I suspect that is because they know they can’t be caught. Most of them amble along, taking their time a few yards ahead of the dogs that flounder in deep snow. Put a crust on that snow, though, and hares will pick up enough speed to keep just ahead of the pack. Generally hares run a wide circle, returning to the same vicinity where the dogs started them. But not always. I’ve seen hares lope through the woods for a mile on a course as straight as a Nebraska section road. Years ago, Holsinger was hunting a linear strip of woods, between a Michigan Upper Peninsula highway and Lake Superior, when his dogs jump-started a snowshoe. When the rabbit took his dogs out of hearing, Holsinger leaped into his truck and drove two miles to where the cover petered out. Ten minutes later he shot the animal when it came bounding through. Most hares would have crossed the highway at some point; Holsinger’s hunch that this one would not paid off.

On a warm, sunny afternoon you can post an area punctuated by the Y-shaped prints of snowshoes and sometimes get shots at animals sunning themselves. Stillhunting, tracking and stalking are effective ways to hunt them, too, if you remember to move slowly and bend down to rabbit-eye level now and then. Just as quietly moving deer hunters look for the flick of a tail or some other part of a buck’s anatomy, so, too, should hare hunters watch for telltale movements or black-tipped ears on the white-on-white bunnies.

It’s easy to find out if hares are using an area by keeping an eye out for their tracks, trails, droppings and eating signs. Saplings girdled near the ground are pretty good clues that a hungry hare stopped by. If food is plentiful, snowshoes will occupy a five to 10-acre area all winter. But if food is scarce, they will migrate several miles in search of something to eat.

Sometimes hares can be pushovers but not very often. One occasion is during years when their populations are cycling high and the animals don’t exhibit the same degree of caution they do during lean population years. The other time is when a fluke of nature puts all-white hares in snowless woods, a condition that can happen in the late fall or late winter. Then, the rabbits are as easy to see as the Blaze Orange clothing on your hunting partner. Nature always helps wild things to adapt, however, because in portions of Oregon, Washington and British Columbia, where snow is generally scarce, snowshoe hares don’t turn white at all.

No matter where you find the varying hare, the most exciting way to hunt them is with hounds. Best scenting days are when temperatures are near freezing or higher and the snow packs underfoot. Worst conditions are extreme cold and powdery snow because what scent there is gets easily covered by the first dog floundering on the track.

“Only the hounds seem to know if hunting will be good or not,” said Holsinger, who has owned and raised dozens of high-stamina beagles, which are most hare hunters’ dog of choice. For two years a couple of Holsinger’s friends kept careful records, noting such hunting-day conditions as temperature, humidity, wind and dog behavior. Their conclusion? Not only is every day different, but it is often unpredictable. On good-weather days the dogs sometimes had trouble getting a chase going, and then on certain days of poor conditions, they ran well.

“Just listen to those hounds,” Holsinger said as he and I hurried down a logging road next to a swamp where the dogs were puzzling out a fresh track. “We put a new dog in that pack, and the music is sweeter than ever.”

Holsinger was striding along in front of me in a place where the woods necked down. Bouncing from one side of his game bag was the white head of a hare. Sticking from the other side were the fuzzy feet of another snowshoe. “The dogs are turning this way,” he said, looking back at me. “Where do you want to set up?”

Read Next: A Christmas Hunt for the Black Hare of Halcott Mountain

“I’ll take a stand right here,” I said and waved him on. “I have a hunch the rabbit will cross at this bottleneck.”

It didn’t. Instead, the hare loped across the road in front of Holsinger, who bowled it over with a load of 12-gauge, No. 5 shot.

It just wasn’t my day for hunches, but all was not lost. I knew where to get another wedge of hot raspberry pie.

#8367. Spanish Team Bags First Ascent of Jugal II

Mikel Zabalza, Ruben Perez, and Mikel Saez de Urabain have completed the first ascent of 6,518m Jugal II.

According to Spanish media, the team climbed via the east-southeast side and reached the summit on October 26. One day later, they returned to base camp, their home team told Diario de Navarra. Zabalza and Urabain had explored the area in the spring of 2024, but bad weather prevented them from attempting the peak. The team will share more details when they’re back home.

Jugal II was also the planned goal for Italians Nives Meroi and Romano Benet, who left for the area three weeks ago. Originally, the team wanted to climb Tilicho Peak in the Annapurna region. Recent storms and floods had cut trails and swept away bridges in that area, so they had to seek an alternative.

ExplorersWeb caught up with Meroi as she and Benet reached a lodge to seek shelter from the heavy rain.

“We’re on our way to Kathmandu, and we are with the Spaniards,” she confirmed. As Nives explained, they all attempted the climb, and the Spanish team reached the summit, while the Italians retreated on the previous day. Until now, there has been no news from the Italians since Tine Cuder of Slovenia, the third team member, fell ill and left the expedition two weeks ago.

Left to right, Nives Meroi, Tine Cuder, and Romano Benet in Kathmandu. Photo: Romano Benet

The Jugal Himal is just northeast of Kathmandu, on the Tibetan border. Surprisingly accessible for a previously unclimbed peak, it’s reachable by bus and a few days’ trekking. Jugal I and II opened to foreign expeditions in 2023. In spring 2024, veteran South Korean climber Um Hong-gil led a Korean-Nepalese expedition featuring Sherpa celebrities Dawa Yangzum and Lakpa Dendi to both unclimbed Jugals. They successfully summited Jugal I, but not Jugal II. According to The Himalayan Database, Jugal II remained unclimbed.

The main peaks in Jugal Himal. Photo: Nepali News Hub

#8364. Piolets d'Or Insider: How the Jury Works, Style Debates, and Future Plans

The recent 2026 edition of the Piolets d’Or awards, held last week in a remote corner of the French Alps, felt like an organization trying to adapt to fast-changing times and attract larger audiences while keeping its prestige and spirit intact.

ExplorersWeb was there to meet old acquaintances and to put a face to some of the names we wrote about in the last 12 months. We also wanted to participate in the collective exercise of reflection about the future.

Views of Les Ecrins Massif from Saint-Christophe-en-Oisans. Photo: Angela Benavides

Piolet d’Or recipients enjoyed a relaxed atmosphere at the tiny village of Saint-Christophe-en-Oisans and a ceremony at Burg d’Oisans, a 30-minute drive down the valley. Yet, the most interesting event took place the following day, as an elite group of climbers sat around a table in a small hall with large glass windows facing autumn-colored forests and the ragged peaks of the Ecrins Massif, covered in the first snow dust of the season.

Representing the awardees were Nicolas Jean (awarded for climbing Jannu East with Benjamin Vedrines); the complete teams from Ultar Shar, Aikache Chokk, and Jerupaja Grande; a hyper-energetic, widely smiling Peter Habeler, 84, who received a lifetime achievement Piolet d’Or; Simon Welfringer, who gave a talk; organizers Christian Trommsdorf and David Chambre; geographer and chronicler Rodolphe Popier, and two members of the jury: Jordi Corminas of Spain and Paul Ramsden of the UK. At a press conference, these experts debated some of the hot issues in today’s mountaineering.

Simon Welfringer of France speaks at the post-Piolets d’Or experts’ panel. Photo: Angela Benavides

Trommsdorf noted that the jury had an easy time selecting the awarded climbs this year. He explained how these expert jurists choose the best alpine-style activities of the year.

The members work remotely, choosing from a Big List of outstanding activities. This list is previously compiled by Lindsay Griffin, long-time editor of the American Alpine Journal, and the UK’s Alpine Club. Jurors study the climbs and narrow it down to a short list of candidates, which is not made public. The awards go to those activities chosen by the majority of jury members. In this case, decisions were finalized on the first vote, with no need for a tie-break.

Left to right, Rodolphe Popier, Jordi Corominas, Paul Ramsden (speaking), and David Chambre. Photo: Piotr Drozdz

That led to the first topic of debate: It was noted that some climbing teams happily announce themselves as “Piolet d’Or nominates” on social media when their climbs appear on the Big List — although organizers make it clear that not all activities on that list are suitable for a Piolet d’Or. Yet, no one supported the idea of making the short lists public. The general agreement was to keep the small “best of the year” finalists available only to the jury.

The second topic for debate was the presence of a relatively new piece of technology now ubiquitous on expeditions: drones. These have become essential on rescues, but climbing teams also use them to scout the route ahead. In the near future, drones could also carry supplies, emergency kits, or extra equipment. Commercial outfitters are already using them in this way.

Benjamin Vedrines and Nicolas Jean of France used drones to check the state of their planned route on Jannu. However, they explained that the drone was useless in relaying information about a section that they couldn’t see from Base Camp. It had a different angle of view, and the drone lost connection when it tried to approach that area.

Drones piloted by their base camp film crew also hovered overhead as they traversed the long summit ridge. Finally, before the summit push, they used drones to clearly identify the highest point, to make sure they reached the true summit.

The Ultar Sar team also had a drone, they noted. All the awarded climbers agreed that drones are okay as long as the climbers are completely transparent about what they used them for. Jordi Corominas said the drones are a technological innovation that has come to stay, no different than InReach devices, satphones, or even ice axes and crampons.

Jordi Corominas, left, discusses past climbs with Benjamin Vedrines. Photo: Piotr Drozdz

Interestingly, one jurist stood against the tide: Paul Ramsden is an advocate for the pure alpine-style criteria of the UK climbing school, and with five Piolets d’Or, he is the overall record holder of these prestigious awards. In his opinion, drones spoil the adventure and uncertainty inherent in pure alpine style. Ramsden himself uses neither drones, trackers, nor even satphones.

Finally, Trommsdor suggested possibly expanding the awards to create a special Piolet d’Or for the best rock climb and perhaps even the best ski descent. The idea expand on the new performance category introduced this year in the big list as a test. The category featured, among others, the two Everest ski descents in 2025. Both were heavily supported, and Jim Morrison‘s descent of the Hornbein Couloir was oxygen-assisted.

In the end, one of the performance ski descents received the female award: Typhaine Duperier‘s alpine-style climb+ski descent of Nanga Parbat’s Schell route, with Boris Langenstein.

It is unclear whether the new additions will become official in the near future, but some attendees expressed concern about the context in which these take place. Would they award ski expeditions for their boldness or technical excellence without bearing in mind how the skiers reached the start of their descent (supported climbs, fixed routes, even helicopters)?

As for rock climbs: where to set the difference between a rock climb and an alpine climb on high, but dry, faces? The debate was left open. We will find out what, if anything, changes in the next edition of the Piolets d’Or.

Buried houses at the now abandoned village of La Berarde. Photo: Piotr Drozdz

The physical award is no longer an actual piolet (ice axe). In the last few years, it has been a hand-crafted trophy that changes with the venue. This time, it was a plaque with a reproduction of Ecrins National Park’s most distinctive peak, La Meige. It rested on a piece of rock from the remains of La Berarde, a nearby village destroyed in a flood two years ago.

At the Piolets d’Or ceremony in Burg d’Oisans. Photo: Angela Benavides

Next year, the Piolets d’Or will be staged in the same location, perhaps in late summer. The event will commemorate the 150th anniversary of the first ascent of La Meige. The long-term plan is to turn the Piolet d’Or ceremony into a bigger, international mountain festival.
